headline: Peter Kent (Ninety One) argues the traditional DM/EM distinction in fixed income is breaking down as EM fiscal discipline improves while DM sovereigns deteriorate.
reasoning: Kent contends that post-GFC central bank suppression of volatility is over, and that structurally higher volatility is now the regime. Emerging markets have improved their policy credibility and fiscal discipline, while developed markets have gone the other way. He argues investors should assess bonds on what they contribute to a portfolio — cyclical exposure, yield, defensive co-movement — rather than by geographical/economic labels. He coined the phrase 'unification of DM' following the UK Gilts crisis of September 2022 to capture this convergence.
quote: I think there's a secular theme that's happening at the moment. Um, as you mentioned, the rules of fixed income investing have been changing. I think what you saw post GFC was a period where central banks didn't have to worry about inflation, bought a lot of developed market bonds where the credit or sovereign. So volatility was suppressed for a long, long time. Inflation has become a little bit of a more of a problem since then. Central banks don't have the ability to suppress volatility. Emerging markets on average have improved policy, have improved credibility. Developed markets on average have gone the other way. So what you're seeing is a blurring of lines between emerging markets and developing markets.
episode_title: The emerging edge in fixed income

headline: Ninety One's Peter Kent sees compelling opportunities in EM local currency bonds and hard currency high yield as structural case plays out and flows accelerate
reasoning: Peter Kent argues that emerging markets went through a disappointing decade from 2012, marked by the taper tantrum in 2013, the Fragile Five dynamic, and external imbalances that weighed heavily on EM FX. He notes that over the past five years institutional investors have been curious but skeptical, but over the past two years the structural investment case has been visibly playing out. As evidence mounts, investor sentiment has shifted from skepticism to conviction, and flows into both EM debt and EM equities have been rising in 2024 and 2025. Kent specifically highlights EM local currency bonds and hard currency high yield as areas of particularly interesting opportunity right now.
quote: So from our perspective, there's some really, really interesting opportunities in emerging market local currencies and in high yield hard currencies. I've been on the road seeing clients in Australia for the last few days, and emerging markets were disappointing for a decade from 2012, if you recall. We had the taper tantrum back in 2013 and it was the time of the Fragile Five. So emerging markets were externally out of balance back then, and they eame FX partly because of the dollar, partly because of this imbalance. FX had a tough decade. So I would say over the last five years, institutional investors have been curious but a little bit skeptical. I would say that over the last two years, when people see the evidence of the structural case playing out, they've become a lot more sympathetic to the investment case. So, you know, we've seen people allocating. You can see emerging market debt and emerging market equities have been getting inflows last year and this year. So that skepticism of a tough, tough decade is actually turning into a very solid investment case. And the flows are following.
episode_title: The emerging edge in fixed income

headline: Peter Kent sees a structurally higher interest rate and volatility regime driven by inflation and rising capital demand from hyperscalers and AI investment.
reasoning: Kent argues that the complete reversal of the post-GFC low-rate environment is underway. The demand for capital from hyperscalers and the broader shift in investment mean longer-term rates have had to move higher. This structurally raises volatility, particularly in what were previously considered 'defensive' developed market bonds. He contrasts this with emerging markets, which have behaved consistently throughout this period.
quote: I think 2022 was the case in point. Right? I think we had unprecedented volatility. We had a hiking cycle in the developed markets like we haven't seen for some time. So there is clearly monetary policy volatility because of the inflation outlook. But then what I think we're also seeing is a complete reversal of the low rate environment that we had post GFC. We've seen a shift in investment. We see all of these hyperscalers issuing IPOs. There's a demand for capital out there. So as a result of that you know longer term rates have also had to shift higher. And and and as a result you're going to have greater volatility. Interestingly emerging markets have behaved like they've always behaved throughout this whole thing. The change in volatility is more in the defensive space rather than the emerging space.
episode_title: The emerging edge in fixed income

headline: Peter Kent warns that longer-dated developed market duration no longer provides the portfolio diversification benefits it once did.
reasoning: Kent argues that supply shocks have become a persistent feature of the global economy, which undermines the traditional negative correlation between long-duration government bonds and risk assets. A longer-dated treasury is now considerably more risky from a volatility perspective than in the past and does not offer the correlation benefits investors historically relied on. He encourages investors to rethink bonds based on what they actually introduce to a portfolio rather than defaulting to DM sovereigns as a defensive anchor.
quote: A longer data treasury, for example, is considerably more risky from a volatility perspective than in the past. It doesn't necessarily offer you the correlation benefits you've had in the past. With the advent of supply shocks that have been hitting the globe for some time now. Longer dated duration doesn't function like it used to. So I would sort of ask investors and your viewers to think about bonds and assets, about what they introduce to your portfolio in terms of cyclical defensive co movement, rather than thinking of em as a, as a sort of bad, a backwater of bad policies and bad and bad politics.
episode_title: The emerging edge in fixed income

headline: Peter Kent sees compelling opportunities in EM local currency bonds and hard currency high yield given supportive global growth backdrop.
reasoning: Kent notes that cyclical risk globally appears to be in a good place, supported by both tech investment and broad manufacturing growth. In a good-growth environment he favours long cyclical, high-yielding assets, and EM offers both local currency and hard-currency high yield options that fit this profile. He explicitly identifies EM local currencies and high yield hard currencies as the most interesting opportunities currently available.
quote: When we look at the globe, cyclical risk seems to be in a good place. Some of that admittedly, is driven by tech investment, but manufacturing globally seems quite broad. So in an environment where growth is pretty good, you generally want to be long cyclical assets. You want to be long, high yielding assets. Emerging markets got a lot of those in both local currency and in high yields. So from our perspective, there's some really, really interesting opportunities in emerging market local currencies and in high yield hard currencies.
episode_title: The emerging edge in fixed income

headline: Peter Kent highlights that EM sovereigns have demonstrated superior fiscal discipline and monetary policy orthodoxy compared to DM peers over the past decade.
reasoning: Kent points to Argentina as an extreme example of EM fiscal reform, noting that if Argentina can get its fiscal house in order it says a lot about the broader EM shift. EM countries have shown restraint in government spending, responded earlier and more decisively to inflation than DM central banks who called it transitory, and have increasingly issued debt in local currency — reducing the 'original sin' of dollar borrowing. This improved credibility makes EM bonds arguably more attractive than DM on a structural basis.
quote: Who would have thought that Argentina would have been the economic poster child. So if, if, if they can, if they can get their fiscal ducks in a row, then you know, that says a lot. So what we have seen over the last decade is an is fiscal restraint in emerging markets. They haven't been as profligate as the developed markets. You've seen monetary policy orthodoxy when inflation turned up in developed markets. They called it transitory. When it turned up in emerging markets, they did what they had to do. We've seen a lot more issuance in emerging markets, in local currency. That tells you that those countries are credible enough to issue in local currency. That means the original sin of borrowing in dollars is mitigated.
episode_title: The emerging edge in fixed income
